_comment: Birds (scripts/sim/birds.gd), just for looking at: they never affect ships. Two systems. gulls: every port has a flock circling it, grain and livestock carriers always have one over them, other ships, and pods of sea animals, sometimes; flocks of 3-25, busiest at dawn and dusk and quietest at night (by the sun where they are), bigger in each hemisphere's breeding season and around ships loading or unloading. seabirds: when a ship at sea is where a species is that month, now and then some take up following it for a few hours. Each species is where one of its seasons' ranges ([lon from, lon to, lat from, lat to]) covers, in that season's months (all year when it has no months); gulls in no range at a port, the nearest species' range stands in. span is the wingspan drawn, in dock units (ships are 3-14 long); colors: mantle (back and upper wings), head, tip (wingtips), belly and bill. behavior (seabirds): soar (wide slow circles), glide (sweeping arcs behind a ship), dart (quick flaps, hovering), line (a file alongside, low over the water) or skim (stiff-winged, low, weaving behind). follow: [chance a ship is followed in a stretch of follow_hours, fewest, most]. raptors (eagles, hawks, the osprey) never follow ships: they live along the shore, and a port in a species' range that month has some about it by day, in stretches of raptor_hours (visit: [chance a port has them in a stretch, fewest, most]), each going about it as it really does: snatch (a sea eagle: sits on its perch on the shore, now and then flies out and swoops to snatch a fish off the surface, and takes it back), plunge (the osprey: circles over the water, hovers, plunges feet first and carries its fish head forward to a perch to eat), stoop (soars high over the land and dives steeply), kite (circles on thermals over the land and hangs still on the wind, hunting below), kettle (Swainson's hawks migrating: a flock circling up on a thermal, then streaming off), pack (Harris's hawks: perched together, then hunting low over the land in a line, taking turns to lead) or perch (a goshawk or Cooper's hawk: sits hidden on the shore, then dashes off low, flap-flap-glide); tail and shoulder colors are optional. sea_ducks (eiders and scoters) raft on the sea off ports where a species is that month, in stretches of sea_duck_hours, day and night (raft: [chance a port has a raft in a stretch, fewest, most]): bobbing, diving for mussels (scoters with sync dive all together), now and then the raft takes off and flies low in a line to settle somewhere new; in a season marked moving they are migrating, and pass in long low lines over the sea instead; creche: in high summer hens lead their pooled ducklings; colors: mantle (back), sides, head, cap, and optional nape, breast, patch (on the head), wing (a patch), bill, hen (the hens are this brown). cormorants (in stretches of cormorant_hours, group: [chance a port has them in a stretch, fewest, most]): about a port, some stand on its breakwater (by day now and then holding their wings out to dry; all of them roosting there at night), some swim low off it and make long dives for fish, and now and then a flock flies past low over the water in a V; colors as the seabirds', plus cheek (a pale face patch) and throat. Birds that fly in Vs in life do so here: pelicans following ships, cormorants passing, and eiders and scoters on migration. where is said in the field guide. land_animals: the land animals (living on the map as the wildlife: data/wildlife.json has their sizes, homes and ways), in groups of group [fewest, most] (young: the share after the first that are young, drawn small and kept close to their mother). habits is said in the field guide; group_word and young_word name the group and its young in its popup ("a pride of 6 with 2 cubs").

herring.name: Herring Gull
herring.where: North Atlantic coasts of Europe and North America, all year.
herring.fact: Chicks peck the red spot on their parent's bill to make it bring up food.

great_black_backed.name: Great Black-backed Gull
great_black_backed.where: North Atlantic coasts, from New England to Norway.
great_black_backed.fact: The biggest gull in the world, with a wingspan of up to 1.7 m.

lesser_black_backed.name: Lesser Black-backed Gull
lesser_black_backed.where: Northern Europe in summer; south to the Mediterranean and West Africa in winter.
lesser_black_backed.fact: Many now winter around Europe's cities instead of flying to Africa.

yellow_legged.name: Yellow-legged Gull
yellow_legged.where: The Mediterranean, the Black Sea and Atlantic Iberia, all year.
yellow_legged.fact: The Mediterranean's big gull, named for the bright yellow legs that tell it from the Herring Gull.

black_headed.name: Black-headed Gull
black_headed.where: Europe and Asia; further south in winter, to Africa, India and Southeast Asia.
black_headed.fact: Its 'black' summer hood is really chocolate brown, and it loses it in winter.

ring_billed.name: Ring-billed Gull
ring_billed.where: North America, the Great Lakes above all; south to the Gulf and Mexico in winter.
ring_billed.fact: The gull of North American car parks: there are millions of them, mostly inland.

laughing.name: Laughing Gull
laughing.where: The US Atlantic and Gulf coasts and the Caribbean; south to Brazil in winter.
laughing.fact: Named for its call, a long cackling 'ha-ha-ha-ha'.

california.name: California Gull
california.where: Western North America's Pacific coast, from Mexico to Canada.
california.fact: Utah's state bird: flocks saved the early settlers' crops from a plague of crickets in 1848.

western.name: Western Gull
western.where: The Pacific coast from Washington to Baja California, all year.
western.fact: Almost never seen more than a few kilometres inland or out to sea.

glaucous_winged.name: Glaucous-winged Gull
glaucous_winged.where: The North Pacific: Alaska, British Columbia, Kamchatka and northern Japan.
glaucous_winged.fact: Its wingtips are grey, not black, the same pale grey as the rest of its wings.

black_tailed.name: Black-tailed Gull
black_tailed.where: The coasts of Japan, Korea and eastern China.
black_tailed.fact: Japan calls it umineko, 'sea cat', for its mewing call.

heermanns.name: Heermann's Gull
heermanns.where: The Gulf of California and Mexico's Pacific coast; north to California after breeding.
heermanns.fact: Almost all of them nest on one small island, Isla Rasa, in the Gulf of California.

sooty.name: Sooty Gull
sooty.where: The Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, the Persian Gulf and the Arabian Sea.
sooty.fact: Dark brown all over but for a white collar: a gull of hot, dry coasts.

kelp.name: Kelp Gull
kelp.where: The Southern Hemisphere: South America, southern Africa, New Zealand and the Antarctic Peninsula.
kelp.fact: Off Argentina some have learned to peck at the backs of right whales as they surface.

silver.name: Silver Gull
silver.where: Australia, New Zealand and New Caledonia, all year.
silver.fact: Australia's everyday gull, as at home on a beach as at a fish-and-chip shop.

andean_condor.name: Andean Condor
andean_condor.where: Down the west coast of South America, along the Andes from Colombia to Patagonia.
andean_condor.fact: One of the biggest flying birds, with wings over 3 m across: it can soar for hours without a flap.

california_condor.name: California Condor
california_condor.where: The central California coast, around Big Sur.
california_condor.fact: Down to 27 birds in 1987, all taken into care; hundreds fly free again today.

wandering_albatross.name: Wandering Albatross
wandering_albatross.where: Round the Southern Ocean, between about 30 and 60 degrees south, all year.
wandering_albatross.fact: The widest wings of any living bird, up to 3.5 m: some fly round the world in under 50 days.

black_browed_albatross.name: Black-browed Albatross
black_browed_albatross.where: The Southern Ocean; north along South America and southern Africa in the southern winter.
black_browed_albatross.fact: The commonest albatross, and the one most often seen following ships.

laysan_albatross.name: Laysan Albatross
laysan_albatross.where: The North Pacific, from Hawaii to Japan and Alaska.
laysan_albatross.fact: Wisdom, a Laysan Albatross on Midway, is over 70 and still raising chicks: the oldest wild bird known.

arctic_tern.name: Arctic Tern
arctic_tern.where: The Arctic in the northern summer, the Antarctic in the southern summer, down the Atlantic in between.
arctic_tern.fact: It sees more daylight than any other animal, flying from pole to pole and back every year: some 70,000 km.

common_tern.name: Common Tern
common_tern.where: North America, Europe and Asia in summer; the coasts of Africa, South America and southern Asia in winter.
common_tern.fact: Hovers over the water, then plunges in head first after small fish.

caspian_tern.name: Caspian Tern
caspian_tern.where: Coasts and big lakes on every continent but Antarctica and South America: the Great Lakes, the Baltic and the Caspian in summer, the Gulf of Mexico, West Africa and India in winter; all year in Australia, New Zealand and southern Africa.
caspian_tern.fact: The biggest tern in the world, as big as a gull, with a thick blood-red bill.

royal_tern.name: Royal Tern
royal_tern.where: Warm Atlantic and Pacific coasts of the Americas, from Virginia and California down to Argentina and Peru, and the coast of West Africa; the northern ones go south in winter.
royal_tern.fact: Its shaggy black crest shrinks to a white forehead after the breeding season.

brown_pelican.name: Brown Pelican
brown_pelican.where: The coasts of the Americas, from California and Carolina to Peru and Brazil.
brown_pelican.fact: Dives from 20 m up to scoop fish in its throat pouch, which holds 10 litres.

great_white_pelican.name: Great White Pelican
great_white_pelican.where: Africa, the eastern Mediterranean, the Black Sea and India.
great_white_pelican.fact: Flocks fish together, herding fish into a ring before scooping them up.

australian_pelican.name: Australian Pelican
australian_pelican.where: Australia and New Guinea, all year.
australian_pelican.fact: It has the longest bill of any bird, up to half a metre.

sooty_shearwater.name: Sooty Shearwater
sooty_shearwater.where: Breeds round New Zealand, Chile and the Falklands in the southern summer; spends the northern summer in the North Pacific and North Atlantic.
sooty_shearwater.fact: Flies a giant figure of eight round the Pacific each year: some 64,000 km.

manx_shearwater.name: Manx Shearwater
manx_shearwater.where: Britain, Ireland and the North Atlantic in summer; off Brazil and Argentina in winter.
manx_shearwater.fact: One bird ringed on Bardsey Island lived over 50 years and flew some 8 million km.

great_cormorant.name: Great Cormorant
great_cormorant.where: Coasts, lakes and rivers of Europe, Asia, Africa, Australia and New Zealand, and the North Atlantic coast of North America; the northern ones go south for the winter.
great_cormorant.fact: Fishermen in China and Japan have trained them to catch fish for over a thousand years.

double_crested_cormorant.name: Double-crested Cormorant
double_crested_cormorant.where: All over North America: the Great Lakes and Canada in summer, the southern US coasts, the Caribbean and Mexico in winter.
double_crested_cormorant.fact: Flocks fly in long lines and Vs low over the water, and can be mistaken for geese.

pelagic_cormorant.name: Pelagic Cormorant
pelagic_cormorant.where: Rocky North Pacific coasts, from California up to Alaska and across to Japan.
pelagic_cormorant.fact: Despite its name it stays near the shore, nesting on sheer sea cliffs.

european_shag.name: European Shag
european_shag.where: Rocky coasts of the North Atlantic and the Mediterranean, from Norway to Morocco.
european_shag.fact: It dives deeper than most cormorants, to 45 m, chasing fish along the bottom.

neotropic_cormorant.name: Neotropic Cormorant
neotropic_cormorant.where: From Texas and Mexico down through the Caribbean and all of South America.
neotropic_cormorant.fact: Flocks sometimes fish together, driving fish into the shallows.

cape_cormorant.name: Cape Cormorant
cape_cormorant.where: The coasts of South Africa and Namibia.
cape_cormorant.fact: Flies out to sea in long lines tens of thousands strong, following the shoals of sardines.

japanese_cormorant.name: Japanese Cormorant
japanese_cormorant.where: Rocky coasts of Japan, Korea and eastern China.
japanese_cormorant.fact: The bird used in Japan's 1,300-year-old ukai: cormorant fishing by torchlight on the rivers.

little_pied_cormorant.name: Little Pied Cormorant
little_pied_cormorant.where: Australia, New Zealand, New Guinea and Indonesia.
little_pied_cormorant.fact: Often fishes alone in the shallows, while the bigger cormorants work deeper water.

guanay_cormorant.name: Guanay Cormorant
guanay_cormorant.where: The coasts of Peru and northern Chile, on the cold Humboldt Current.
guanay_cormorant.fact: Its colonies of millions laid the guano that Peru once exported round the world.

common_eider.name: Common Eider
common_eider.where: Northern coasts round the Arctic and North Atlantic: Scotland, Norway, Iceland, Greenland, Maine and Alaska; south along them in winter.
common_eider.fact: Its down, gathered from abandoned nests, fills the warmest quilts in the world; hens pool their ducklings in creches guarded by 'aunties'.

king_eider.name: King Eider
king_eider.where: The high Arctic tundra in summer; the Bering Sea, Labrador, Greenland and northern Norway in winter.
king_eider.fact: Dives over 50 m for shellfish, and gathers in rafts of tens of thousands on its way north.

spectacled_eider.name: Spectacled Eider
spectacled_eider.where: Alaska's and Siberia's Arctic coasts in summer; the whole world population winters in a few holes in the Bering Sea ice.
spectacled_eider.fact: Its winter home was only found in 1995: hundreds of thousands packed into open water in the pack ice. Listed as threatened since 1993, after Alaska's breeding birds fell by over 90%. As the Bering Sea warms and its ice thins, the clams it dives for are dwindling: its future depends on the Arctic's food chain.

stellers_eider.name: Steller's Eider
stellers_eider.where: Arctic Siberia and Alaska in summer; the Alaska Peninsula, the Aleutians and Norway's Varangerfjord in winter.
stellers_eider.fact: The smallest eider: its flocks dive and surface together, packed tight.

common_scoter.name: Common Scoter
common_scoter.where: Tundra lakes from Iceland to Siberia in summer; off the coasts of Britain, France, Iberia and Morocco in winter.
common_scoter.fact: Its winter rafts off Britain can be tens of thousands strong, a long black line on the sea.

black_scoter.name: Black Scoter
black_scoter.where: Alaska, northern Quebec and eastern Siberia in summer; both coasts of North America and of Japan and Korea in winter.
black_scoter.fact: The drake's mournful whistle carries far over the winter sea.

surf_scoter.name: Surf Scoter
surf_scoter.where: The boreal forests and lakes of Alaska and Canada in summer; North America's Pacific and Atlantic coasts in winter.
surf_scoter.fact: Dives through breaking waves for mussels; its white head patches earn it the name 'skunk-head'.

white_winged_scoter.name: White-winged Scoter
white_winged_scoter.where: Western Canada and Alaska in summer; the Pacific coast from Alaska to California, and New England, in winter.
white_winged_scoter.fact: The biggest scoter: it swallows clams whole and crushes them in its gizzard.

velvet_scoter.name: Velvet Scoter
velvet_scoter.where: Scandinavia and Siberia in summer; the Baltic, the North Sea and the Black Sea in winter.
velvet_scoter.fact: Its white wing patches flash as the whole flock beats low over the waves.

grey_heron.name: Grey Heron
grey_heron.where: Coasts, rivers and marshes across Europe, Asia and Africa, all year; the northernmost go south for the winter.
grey_heron.fact: It can stand stock still for an hour waiting for a fish, then strike in a blink.

great_blue_heron.name: Great Blue Heron
great_blue_heron.where: Coasts and wetlands all over North America, Central America and the Caribbean; the northern ones go south for the winter.
great_blue_heron.fact: Special bones in its neck let it strike at prey in an instant.

purple_heron.name: Purple Heron
purple_heron.where: Reedbeds and marshes of southern Europe, Africa and southern Asia; the European ones winter in Africa.
purple_heron.fact: Shyer than the Grey Heron, it hides in tall reeds, its striped neck blending into the stems.

goliath_heron.name: Goliath Heron
goliath_heron.where: Coasts, lakes and rivers of Africa south of the Sahara, the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf.
goliath_heron.fact: The biggest heron in the world, standing 1.5 m tall; it can catch fish too big to swallow and lose them to fish eagles.

black_crowned_night_heron.name: Black-crowned Night Heron
black_crowned_night_heron.where: Wetlands and harbours on every continent but Australia and Antarctica.
black_crowned_night_heron.fact: It hunts at dusk and through the night, and roosts hunched in trees by day.

striated_heron.name: Striated Heron
striated_heron.where: Mangroves and rocky shores through the tropics: Africa, southern Asia, Australia and South America.
striated_heron.fact: It drops bits of bread or feathers on the water as bait, then grabs the fish that come to look.

great_egret.name: Great Egret
great_egret.where: Warm coasts and wetlands all round the world: the Americas, southern Europe, Africa, Asia and Australia.
great_egret.fact: Hunted nearly to extinction for its lacy breeding plumes, it became the symbol of the National Audubon Society.

little_egret.name: Little Egret
little_egret.where: Coasts and estuaries of Europe, Africa, Asia and Australia; it has spread north to Britain since the 1990s.
little_egret.fact: It stirs up the mud with its bright yellow feet to flush out fish and shrimps.

snowy_egret.name: Snowy Egret
snowy_egret.where: Coasts and marshes of the Americas, from the US south to Argentina; the northern ones winter further south.
snowy_egret.fact: Known for its golden slippers: black legs and bright yellow feet it shuffles to startle prey.

cattle_egret.name: Cattle Egret
cattle_egret.where: Fields and pastures by the coast on every continent but Antarctica; it reached the Americas from Africa by itself in the 1870s.
cattle_egret.fact: It follows cattle and tractors across the fields, snapping up the insects they stir up.

reddish_egret.name: Reddish Egret
reddish_egret.where: Shallow lagoons of the Gulf of Mexico, Florida, the Caribbean and Baja California.
reddish_egret.fact: It dances through the shallows, lurching and spinning with its wings held out as a shade to see fish.

eurasian_bittern.name: Eurasian Bittern
eurasian_bittern.where: Reedbeds across Europe and Asia; northern ones winter in southern Europe, Africa and southern Asia.
eurasian_bittern.fact: The male's booming call, like someone blowing over a bottle, carries 5 km across the marsh.

american_bittern.name: American Bittern
american_bittern.where: Marshes across Canada and the northern US in summer; the southern US, Mexico and the Caribbean in winter.
american_bittern.fact: Its gulping pump-er-lunk call has earned it the names thunder-pumper and stake-driver.

least_bittern.name: Least Bittern
least_bittern.where: Marshes of the eastern US, Mexico, the Caribbean and South America.
least_bittern.fact: One of the smallest herons in the world, light enough to clamber up a reed stem gripping it with its toes.

australasian_bittern.name: Australasian Bittern
australasian_bittern.where: Reedy swamps of southern Australia and New Zealand.
australasian_bittern.fact: Endangered: only a few thousand are left, as the wetlands they need have been drained.

common_crane.name: Common Crane
common_crane.where: Breeds in the marshes of northern Europe and Siberia; winters in Spain, North Africa, the Middle East, India and China.
common_crane.fact: Tens of thousands stop at Lake Hornborga in Sweden every spring to dance before they nest.

sandhill_crane.name: Sandhill Crane
sandhill_crane.where: Breeds across Canada, Alaska and eastern Siberia; winters in California, Texas, Florida and Mexico.
sandhill_crane.fact: Its fossils go back millions of years; half a million gather on Nebraska's Platte River each March.

red_crowned_crane.name: Red-crowned Crane
red_crowned_crane.where: Hokkaido in Japan all year; northeast China and Russia in summer, wintering on the coasts of Korea and eastern China.
red_crowned_crane.fact: A symbol of luck and long life in East Asia; Japanese tradition says folding a thousand paper cranes grants a wish.

whooping_crane.name: Whooping Crane
whooping_crane.where: Winters on the Texas Gulf coast at Aransas, and flies 4,000 km to Wood Buffalo in northern Canada to breed.
whooping_crane.fact: Down to just 15 birds in 1941, careful protection has brought it back to about 800: the tallest bird in North America.

grey_crowned_crane.name: Grey Crowned Crane
grey_crowned_crane.where: Wetlands and grasslands of eastern and southern Africa, from Kenya and Uganda down to South Africa.
grey_crowned_crane.fact: Uganda's national bird, on its flag; one of the only cranes that roosts in trees.

sarus_crane.name: Sarus Crane
sarus_crane.where: Wetlands and paddy fields of India, Cambodia and Vietnam, and northern Australia.
sarus_crane.fact: The tallest flying bird in the world, up to 1.8 m; pairs mate for life and call in duet.

brolga.name: Brolga
brolga.where: Wetlands of northern and eastern Australia, and southern New Guinea.
brolga.fact: Famous for its dance, which Aboriginal peoples copy in their own ceremonial dances.

bald_eagle.name: Bald Eagle
bald_eagle.where: North America, along coasts, rivers and lakes: Alaska and British Columbia above all.
bald_eagle.fact: Builds the biggest nests of any bird in North America, up to 3 m deep.

white_tailed_eagle.name: White-tailed Eagle
white_tailed_eagle.where: Norway, Iceland, the Baltic and Scotland's west coast, east across Russia to Japan.
white_tailed_eagle.fact: Called the 'flying barn door' for its broad, square wings.

stellers_sea_eagle.name: Steller's Sea Eagle
stellers_sea_eagle.where: Kamchatka and the Sea of Okhotsk in summer; Hokkaido's drift ice in winter.
stellers_sea_eagle.fact: The heaviest eagle in the world, at up to 9 kg, with a huge orange bill.

african_fish_eagle.name: African Fish Eagle
african_fish_eagle.where: Coasts, lakes and rivers of Africa south of the Sahara.
african_fish_eagle.fact: Its ringing cry is called 'the voice of Africa'.

white_bellied_sea_eagle.name: White-bellied Sea Eagle
white_bellied_sea_eagle.where: Coasts from India through Southeast Asia to Australia.
white_bellied_sea_eagle.fact: Pairs keep the same territory, and nest, for years on end.

golden_eagle.name: Golden Eagle
golden_eagle.where: Mountains and wild coasts across the north: Scotland, Norway, Alaska, the Rockies, Japan.
golden_eagle.fact: Stoops on its prey at over 240 km/h.

wedge_tailed_eagle.name: Wedge-tailed Eagle
wedge_tailed_eagle.fact: Australia's biggest bird of prey; its long tail is shaped like a diamond.

osprey.name: Osprey
osprey.where: Coasts, lakes and rivers on every continent but Antarctica: north in summer, south to the tropics in winter; all year in Australia.
osprey.fact: It plunges feet first for fish, and carries them head forward to cut the wind.

red_tailed_hawk.name: Red-tailed Hawk
red_tailed_hawk.where: Across North America, from Alaska to Panama.
red_tailed_hawk.fact: Its scream is the one films give to every eagle.

rough_legged_hawk.name: Rough-legged Hawk
rough_legged_hawk.where: The Arctic tundra in summer; south to the northern US, Europe and Asia in winter.
rough_legged_hawk.fact: Feathered right down to its toes against the Arctic cold.

swainsons_hawk.name: Swainson's Hawk
swainsons_hawk.where: The western plains of North America in summer; the pampas of Argentina in winter, by way of Central America and Panama.
swainsons_hawk.fact: Migrates up to 20,000 km a year, in rising 'kettles' of thousands of birds.

harris_hawk.name: Harris's Hawk
harris_hawk.where: From the deserts of the south-western US down through Central and South America.
harris_hawk.fact: The only hawk that hunts in packs, taking turns to chase, and even standing on each other's backs.

northern_goshawk.name: Northern Goshawk
northern_goshawk.where: The northern forests of Europe, Asia and North America.
northern_goshawk.fact: Weaves through trees at full speed after its prey; Attila the Hun wore one on his helmet.

common_buzzard.name: Common Buzzard
common_buzzard.where: All over Europe, east into Russia; the eastern ones winter in Africa.
common_buzzard.fact: Europe's commonest bird of prey, often seen circling and mewing over fields.

coopers_hawk.name: Cooper's Hawk
coopers_hawk.where: Woods and towns from southern Canada to Mexico.
coopers_hawk.fact: Migrating hawks often stop to rest on ships passing along the coast.

penguin.name: Penguins
penguin.where: Antarctica and the far south: South Georgia, the Falklands, southern Africa and New Zealand.
penguin.fact: Emperor penguins dive past 500 m and hold their breath for over 20 minutes.
penguin.habits: A huddle of a dozen waddling about; now and then one flops down and toboggans along on its belly, or flaps its flippers.

polar_bear.name: Polar bear
polar_bear.where: The Arctic sea ice: Canada, Alaska, Greenland, Svalbard and Siberia.
polar_bear.fact: Its fur isn't white but see-through, and its skin underneath is black.
polar_bear.habits: Alone, or a mother with cubs: it roams far, rears up to sniff the wind, sprawls flat to rest and rolls in the snow to clean its fur.

camel.name: Dromedary camel
camel.where: The Sahara, Arabia and the deserts of the Middle East.
camel.fact: Its hump stores fat, not water; it can drink 100 litres in ten minutes.
camel.habits: A small string plodding across the sand, kneeling down to rest and chewing the cud.

elephant.name: African elephant
elephant.where: The savannas and forests of Africa south of the Sahara.
elephant.fact: The biggest land animal: it can hear other elephants' rumbles through the ground.
elephant.habits: A family herd with its calves, led by the oldest female: they spray themselves with water and toss dust over their backs.

giraffe.name: Giraffe
giraffe.where: The savannas of East and southern Africa.
giraffe.fact: Its neck has just seven bones, the same as ours, each up to 25 cm long.
giraffe.habits: A loose tower of a few, stretching up to browse and splaying their legs wide to drink.

lion.name: Lion
lion.where: The savannas of Africa, and the Gir forest of India.
lion.fact: A lion's roar carries 8 km across the plains.
lion.habits: A pride with cubs, napping most of the day (up to 20 hours), now and then roaring.

zebra.name: Zebra
zebra.where: The grasslands of East and southern Africa.
zebra.fact: No two zebras have the same stripes.
zebra.habits: A herd grazing, kicking up their heels and rolling in the dust.

kangaroo.name: Kangaroo
kangaroo.where: The grasslands and outback of Australia.
kangaroo.fact: It can't walk backwards, and can bound 9 m in one leap.
kangaroo.habits: A mob bounding about, rearing up to box, and stopping to scratch.

koala.name: Koala
koala.where: The eucalyptus forests of eastern Australia.
koala.fact: It sleeps up to 20 hours a day, digesting its eucalyptus leaves.
koala.habits: On its own and mostly asleep; it wakes now and then to chew some leaves and shuffle a little way.

panda.name: Giant panda
panda.where: The mountain bamboo forests of central China.
panda.fact: It eats bamboo up to 14 hours a day, some 12 kg of it.
panda.habits: Alone, munching bamboo, and now and then rolling over a few times on its way somewhere.

tiger.name: Tiger
tiger.where: India, Southeast Asia and the Russian Far East.
tiger.fact: The biggest cat; its stripes run right through to its skin.
tiger.habits: Alone (or a mother with cubs), prowling its patch, stretching, roaring and napping.

bison.name: American bison
bison.where: The Great Plains of North America, Yellowstone above all.
bison.fact: Down to a few hundred in the 1880s; half a million again today.
bison.habits: A herd grazing slowly across the plains, rolling in dust wallows.

moose.name: Moose
moose.where: The northern forests of North America, Scandinavia and Russia.
moose.fact: A fine swimmer: it can dive 6 m for water plants.
moose.habits: Alone, or a cow and her calf, browsing and tossing its head.

brown_bear.name: Brown bear
brown_bear.where: Alaska, western Canada, Scandinavia, Russia and the mountains of Europe and Asia.
brown_bear.fact: Kodiak and grizzly bears are both brown bears.
brown_bear.habits: Alone, or a mother with cubs: it has a favourite tree to rub its back on, rears up to sniff the air, and its cubs tumble about.

reindeer.name: Reindeer (caribou)
reindeer.where: The Arctic tundra and northern forests round the pole.
reindeer.fact: Some herds walk over 5,000 km a year, the longest land migration.
reindeer.habits: A herd on the move across the tundra, grazing the lichen and tossing their antlers.

llama.name: Llama
llama.where: The Andes of Peru, Bolivia, Chile and Argentina.
llama.fact: Kept in the Andes for 4,000 years to carry loads at altitude.
llama.habits: A few together, grazing, and spitting when they're annoyed.

toucan.name: Toucan
toucan.where: The rainforests of Central and South America.
toucan.fact: Its huge bill is light and hollow, and helps it keep cool.
toucan.habits: A small party flitting from perch to perch, pecking at fruit.

gorilla.name: Gorilla
gorilla.habits: A troop round its silverback, sitting about eating; he beats his chest now and then.

orangutan.name: Orangutan
orangutan.where: The rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra.
orangutan.fact: Its name is Malay for 'person of the forest'.
orangutan.habits: Alone, or a mother with her baby, swinging through the trees and hanging about.

kiwi.name: Kiwi
kiwi.fact: Its egg is a fifth of its own weight, among the biggest for its size of any bird.
kiwi.habits: A pair scurrying about, probing the ground with their long bills.

lemur.name: Ring-tailed lemur
lemur.fact: Troops are led by the females.
lemur.habits: A troop bounding about together, sitting up to sunbathe and grooming each other.

water_buffalo.name: Water buffalo
water_buffalo.where: South and Southeast Asia's rivers and rice paddies.
water_buffalo.fact: Over 200 million work and live alongside people.
water_buffalo.habits: A herd grazing and wallowing in the mud to keep cool.

quetzal.name: Resplendent quetzal
quetzal.where: The cloud forests of Central America.
quetzal.fact: Sacred to the Maya and Aztecs; Guatemala's money is named after it.
quetzal.habits: One or a pair, flitting between perches and preening.
